title: macOS: JIT emits AVX on Macs without it, so a darwin-x64 baseline build SIGILLs once code tiers up
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1 (1e3511800), built from `main` for `darwin-x64 --baseline=true`

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin x86_64 — reproduced on two independent machines (see below)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is the **second half** of the pre-AVX2 Mac problem, and it is distinct from #32511.

#32511 / #32512 cover the startup crash: the shipped `bun-darwin-x64-baseline` links the Haswell macOS WebKit, whose bmalloc constructors use BMI2, so it `SIGILL`s before `main()`. oven-sh/WebKit#290 builds the missing Nehalem macOS WebKit and fixes that.

With that artifact in place, bun **starts** on a pre-AVX Mac — and then dies as soon as any code tiers up, because JavaScriptCore's JIT emits AVX regardless of the CPU:

```bash
./bun --version
# 1.4.0  -> rc=0, starts fine

./bun -e 'let s=0; for(let i=0;i<3e7;i++){s+=Math.sqrt(i)*1.000001;} console.log(s)'
# rc=132 -> SIGILL

BUN_JSC_useJIT=0 ./bun -e '...same loop...'
# rc=0   -> works
```

### What is the expected behavior?

A `--baseline` darwin build should run on a CPU without AVX.

### What do you see instead?

`SIGILL` once the JIT tiers up. The crash banner states the problem better than I can — bun's own CPU detection is correct, and JSC ignores it:

```
Bun Canary v1.4.0-canary.1 (1e3511800) macOS x64 (baseline)
macOS v14.6.1
CPU: sse42 popcnt                      <-- no AVX
```

### Additional information

**Root cause** — `Source/JavaScriptCore/assembler/MacroAssemblerX86_64.cpp` hardcodes AVX as present on Darwin instead of asking the CPU:

```cpp
#if OS(DARWIN)
        s_avxCheckState = CPUIDCheckState::Set;   // never checks the CPU
#else
        // CPUID.1:ECX.AVX[28] + OSXSAVE[27] + XCR0[2:1] == 11b
#endif
```

oven-sh/WebKit#198 fixed exactly this for Linux/Windows and guarded the new code with `#if !OS(DARWIN)`, so Darwin kept the assumption. `supportsAVX()` then feeds ~10 VEX-emitting codegen sites. `-march=nehalem` cannot help, because the JIT decides at runtime.

Note AVX2 on Darwin **is** detected correctly, via `sysctlbyname("hw.optional.avx2_0")`. Only AVX is assumed — so Sandy/Ivy Bridge Macs (AVX, no AVX2) are unaffected by this one; it hits Macs with no AVX at all.

**Reproduced on two independent machines:**

| test | Mac Pro 5,1 — Xeon X5690, Westmere, macOS 14.7.8 | Apple M1, x64 bun under Rosetta 2, macOS 14.6.1 |
|---|---|---|
| `bun --version` | rc=0 | rc=0 |
| JIT-heavy loop | **rc=132** | **rc=132** |
| `BUN_JSC_useJIT=0`

excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

`1.3.14+0d9b296af` (also reproducible on current `main`)

### What platform is your computer?

`Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm`

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Create this fixture:

```text
.
├── main.js
└── node_modules
    └── dual-preload
        ├── import.js
        ├── package.json
        └── require.cjs
```

`node_modules/dual-preload/package.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "dual-preload",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "import": "./import.js",
      "require": "./require.cjs"
    }
  }
}
```

`node_modules/dual-preload/import.js`:

```js
console.log("import");
```

`node_modules/dual-preload/require.cjs`:

```js
console.log("require");
```

`main.js`:

```js
console.log("main");
```

Then compare Node 26.4.0 and Bun:

```console
$ node --require dual-preload main.js
require
main

$ bun --require dual-preload main.js
import
main

$ bun --import dual-preload main.js
import
main
```

### What is the expected behavior?

`bun --require dual-preload main.js` should use the package's `require` export condition and print:

```text
require
main
```

This should not be implemented as an extension heuristic. The `--require` preload should resolve with require conditions and execute through CommonJS require semantics, while `--import` should continue using import conditions and the ESM loader.

Node handles these as distinct paths: `--require` calls `Module._preloadModules()`, which creates a parent module rooted at `process.cwd()` and calls `parent.require()`; `--import` uses the ESM loader.

### What do you see instead?

Bun treats `--require`, `--import`, and `--preload` as the same preload kind.

The CLI parser currently flattens all three flags into one `ctx.preloads` array:

https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/blob/main/src/runtime/cli/Arguments.rs#L939-L966

The runtime then resolves every entry with `ImportKind::Stmt` and evaluates it through `JSModuleLoader::import_ptr`:

https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/blob/main/src/runtime/jsc_hooks.rs#L688-L767

As a result, `--require` selects the `import` branch of conditional exports.

### Additional information

Node reference implementation:

- `--require` preload initialization: https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/bf5c2217045fe2e8150c3c9d7d3f311ae60f1eed/lib/internal/process/pre_execution.js#L775-L785
- `Module._preloadModules()`: https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/bf5c2217045fe2e8150c3c9d7d3f311ae60f1eed/lib/internal/modules/cjs/loader.

`Headers.prototype.clear()` for reusing instances without reallocation
excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

Server frameworks that reuse a `Headers` instance across request cycles (e.g. resetting response headers between requests) currently have no way to clear all headers without allocating a new `Headers` object. The workaround — iterating `.keys()` and calling `.delete(key)` — is slower than allocating a new `Headers`, leaving allocation as the only performant option.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Add `Headers.prototype.clear()` to remove all header entries in-place, matching the existing API of `Map.prototype.clear()`, `Set.prototype.clear()`. This allows reusing the same `Headers` instance across request cycles without allocating a new one:

```js
headers.clear();
```

This is a natural extension for a key-value collection type — all other built-in collection types (`Map`, `Set`) already have `clear()`.

### What alternatives have you considered?

1. **Iterate `.keys()` and `.delete()` each header** — works but is slower than `new Headers()` due to JS iterator overhead and per-key hash lookups. Not a viable optimisation.

2. **Reassign `= new Headers()`** — the current approach. Allocates a new internal hash table every request, which shows up as 25%+ of CPU time under load. Wastes memory and GC cycles.

3. **Track dirty keys and delete only those** — adds complexity and bookkeeping overhead that negates the benefit for the small number of headers per request (typically 2-5).

4. **Accept the status quo** — `Headers` is not specified to have `clear()`, so the question is whether a pragmatic non-standard extension is justified. We believe the precedent of `Map.clear()`, `Set.clear()` — all designed by the same Web IDL committee — makes this a natural addition that aligns with existing conventions.

---

## Supporting Data

From CPU profiling a Bun server handling ~16k requests:

- `new Headers()`: **25.2% of total runtime** (17.29s out of 68.39s)
- Iteration workaround (`.keys()` → `.delete()`): slower than `new Headers()` due to JS iterator overhead and per-key hash lookups
- A native `clear()` method would zero the internal hash table in one shot — no allocation, no per-key iteration

title: HMR generates invalid binding for dependency module named `arguments`
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running? Reproduced on both `1.3.9+cf6cdbbb` and `1.3.14` (Linux x64 baseline build). ### What platform is your computer? Linux x86_64 (baseline CPU build required). ### What steps can reproduce the bug? Install `typebox@1.1.38` (also present in current `typebox@1.3.6`) and create: ```html
``` ```ts // client.ts import { Type } from 'typebox'; document.querySelector('#root')!.textContent = Type.String().type; ``` ```ts // server.ts import page from './index.html'; Bun.serve({ port: 3099, routes: { '/': page } }); ``` Run: ```sh bun --hot server.ts ``` Open `http://localhost:3099` in Chromium. ### What is the expected behavior? The client module parses and `#root` contains `string`. ### What do you see instead? The page remains blank. Chromium reports: ```text SyntaxError: Invalid destructuring assignment target ``` Bun's HMR wrapper generates a binding equivalent to: ```js var [arguments, environment, hashing, locale, memory, settings, unreachable] = hmr.imports; ``` for TypeBox's `build/system/arguments/index.mjs` module. `arguments` is not a valid destructuring binding target. The same TypeBox usage works in a production bundle and without the problematic HMR wrapper. It also works under `--hot` when using a dependency whose module graph has no module named `arguments`. ### Additional information This is a parse-time failure, so application error boundaries and console logging cannot surface it. HMR import binding names should be made safe when a resolved module basename is a reserved/restricted identifier (for example by prefixing or indexing generated bindings).

title: fetch() connection-refused error shape differs from Node: no e.cause.code === 'ECONNREFUSED'
excerpt:
## What

When `fetch()` fails because the connection is refused, Bun and Node.js expose the failure through **different error shapes**, which breaks cross-runtime error handling.

- **Node.js**: `err.cause.code === 'ECONNREFUSED'` (the code is nested on `.cause`).
- **Bun**: `err.code === 'ConnectionRefused'` (top-level `.code`; `.cause` is `undefined`).

Code that follows the documented Node/undici shape (`if (err.cause?.code === 'ECONNREFUSED')`) silently never matches under Bun, so a friendly, actionable error message degrades to a raw `"Unable to connect. Is the computer able to access the url?"`.

## Reproduce (Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64)

```js
try {
  await fetch('http://localhost:1/', { method: 'POST' })
} catch (e) {
  console.log('name:', e.name)              // Error
  console.log('message:', e.message)        // "Unable to connect. Is the computer able to access the url?"
  console.log('code:', e.code)              // "ConnectionRefused"
  console.log('cause?.code:', e.cause?.code) // undefined
}
```

Node prints `cause?.code: ECONNREFUSED` and no top-level `.code` for the same call.

## Why it matters

Libraries that want a portable "is this a connection-refused error?" check must special-case Bun:

```js
const isConnectionRefused = e =>
  e?.cause?.code === 'ECONNREFUSED' ||   // Node
  e?.code === 'ConnectionRefused'         // Bun
```

## Ask

Align Bun's `fetch` connection-error shape with Node/undici — ideally exposing the standard `ECONNREFUSED`-style code on `err.cause.code` (and the other `E*` codes: `ECONNRESET`, `ENOTFOUND`, `ETIMEDOUT`, etc.) — or document the Bun shape as intentional so libraries know to check both. Consistency (or documentation) is the fix; either resolves the workaround.

Found while writing cross-runtime tests for a TypeScript toolchain (tjs-lang) whose LLM client runs under both Bun and Node.

title: Async-thrown Error loses its message from error.stack when GC runs before first .stack access
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

Reproduced on 1.2.22 and 1.3.14 (latest at time of filing)

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin arm64 (macOS 25.0.0, Apple Silicon)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```js
// repro.mjs
async function boom() { throw new Error("the message"); }
try {
  await boom();
} catch (e) {
  Bun.gc(true); // any GC between construction and first .stack access — organic idle GC triggers it too
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ message: e.message, stackHead: e.stack.split("\n")[0] }));
}
```

```
$ bun repro.mjs
{"message":"the message","stackHead":"Error"}
```

`e.message` is intact, but the first line of `e.stack` is a bare `Error` — the message never makes it into the materialized stack string.

### What is the expected behavior?

```
{"message":"the message","stackHead":"Error: the message"}
```

which is what Node 22 prints for the same script (with `globalThis.gc` via `--expose-gc`, or with the timer variant below).

### What do you see instead?

`stackHead` is `"Error"` — the message is dropped from the stack string.

### Additional information

Boundary conditions, all verified on both 1.2.22 and 1.3.14:

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| **Async**-thrown (rejection crosses an `await`), GC before first `.stack` read | **message lost** |
| Sync-thrown, same forced GC | correct |
| Async-thrown, `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10))` before read (no forced GC — organic idle GC) | **message lost** |
| Async-thrown, `setTimeout(…, 0)` or a microtask (`await Promise.resolve()`) before read | correct (loop never idles long enough to GC) |
| Async-thrown, `.stack` touched once *before* the GC (primes materialization), read again after | correct |

So the trigger is: an error whose rejection crossed an `await` boundary, plus any GC before the lazy stack string is first materialized. It looks like whatever pre-materialization data backs the message portion of the deferred stack string is not protected from collection on the async path (the sync path is fine). Possibly adjacent to earlier GC-during-stack-materialization fixes (#25096, #31789), but those were crashes — this is silent data loss.

Real-world impact: we hit this in a compiled CLI (`bun build --compile`) where errors are formatted via `err.stack` at top level after async command dispatch — under normal GC pressure roughly 1 in 4 invocations printed error output with no message at all (`Command failed, Error\n    at …`), which made a user-facing auth hint vani

title: bun test: CSS Modules (.scss) loader throws "Unexpected ." parse error, reported async as "Unhandled error between tests" — 1.4.0-canary.1
excerpt:
### Bun version
`1.4.0-canary.1+6ad467f02`

### Platform
Darwin arm64 (macOS), `Darwin 25.5.0`

### Description
After upgrading to a canary build of Bun, `bun test` started failing 2 previously-passing test files with a parse error inside a `.scss` CSS Module — the SCSS appears to be fed to the JS/TS parser instead of the CSS-Modules loader:

```
# Unhandled error between tests
-------------------------------
1 | .addButton {
    ^
error: Unexpected .
    at .../styles.module.scss:1:1
-------------------------------
```

The error surfaces as an *async* "Unhandled error between tests" rather than a synchronous import failure, even though it points at line 1 of the `.scss` file.

### What I've ruled out
- **Not a syntax problem in the file itself.** Copying the exact failing `.scss` file (plain class selectors + Tailwind `@apply`, nested selectors) into an isolated single-file `bun test` repro parses and passes fine.
- **Not flaky.** Fails deterministically across repeated runs, and reproduces running the single affected test file in isolation (not just the full suite).
- **Correlated but not sufficient in isolation:** both failing test files use the documented `mock.module()` hoisting pattern (calling `mock.module('some-package', () => ({...}))` before importing the component under test, where the component's import graph includes the `.scss` file). I was not able to shrink this down to a trivial standalone repro combining `mock.module()` + a sibling `.scss` import + barrel re-exports — it seems to require a larger, real-world import graph to trigger, which suggests a transpiler-cache or async-transpile-path bug rather than a straightforward parser bug (e.g., Bun may still be eagerly/lazily transpiling the real dependency chain behind a `mock.module()`-intercepted import, and that background pass picks the wrong loader for the `.scss` file).

### Impact
Test suite goes from 997/997 passing to 995/997 after the canary bump, with no source changes.

### Ask
Happy to provide a redacted repro package (the two `.scss` files + surrounding component/test structure, no proprietary logic) if that helps narrow it down — let me know what would be most useful to attach.

title: Windows: mkdirSync(path, { recursive: true }) throws EEXIST when the directory has the ReadOnly attribute
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 10 Pro (10.0.19045) x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```js
const fs = require("fs");
const { execSync } = require("child_process");

const dir = "testdir";
fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
execSync(`attrib +R ${dir}`);        // mark the directory ReadOnly

fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });  // <-- throws EEXIST on Bun, fine on Node
```

### What is the expected behavior?

No error. Per the Node docs, `recursive: true` "returns `undefined` even when the directory already exists" and must not throw. Node 24.14.0 runs the snippet above without complaint.

### What do you see instead?

```
EEXIST: file already exists, mkdir 'testdir'
```

### Additional information

The trigger is specifically the **ReadOnly attribute** on the existing directory — not the path, not a reparse point:

| Directory | Attributes | Bun 1.3.14 | Node 24 |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain | `Directory` | OK | OK |
| junction (`mklink /J`) | `Directory, ReparsePoint` | OK | OK |
| plain + ReadOnly | `ReadOnly, Directory` | **EEXIST** | OK |
| junction + ReadOnly | `ReadOnly, Directory, ReparsePoint` | **EEXIST** | OK |

**Why this matters in practice:** OneDrive marks its synced folders `ReadOnly`, so any application installed under OneDrive hits this on startup. That is how I found it — a server failed to boot because an idempotent `mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })` threw EEXIST on its own data directory. The same install runs fine under Node. OneDrive's "Always keep on this device" does not help, since the attribute stays.

This may be related to #29521, which reported the same EEXIST-on-existing-directory behaviour on Windows (1.3.11/1.3.13). It was auto-closed as a duplicate of #21901, but #21901 is about `Promise.all` with `mkdir(".")`, which looks like a different issue. #30264 also reports OneDrive-related trouble on Windows paths.

title: Runtime transpiler cache causes unknown-extension ESM imports to use the TSX loader on a warm cache
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1+8adb8de8b

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

An entry point eligible for Bun's runtime transpiler cache imports an SVG correctly on the first run, but the identical second run incorrectly parses the SVG as TSX.

The entry point must be larger than the cache's 4 KiB minimum. The imported asset itself can be tiny.

```sh
mkdir bun-runtime-cache-repro
cd bun-runtime-cache-repro

printf '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"/>' > asset.svg

bun -e 'await Bun.write("run.ts", `import asset from "./asset.svg";\n/*${"x".repeat(5000)}*/\nconsole.log(asset);\n`)'

export BUN_RUNTIME_TRANSPILER_CACHE_PATH="$(mktemp -d)"

bun run run.ts
bun run run.ts
```

No plugin, mock, or test runner is involved. Setting `BUN_RUNTIME_TRANSPILER_CACHE_PATH=0` also makes repeated runs succeed.

### What is the expected behavior?

Both invocations should behave identically and print the absolute path to `asset.svg`, as specified by Bun's built-in `file` loader:

```text
/path/to/bun-runtime-cache-repro/asset.svg
```

### What do you see instead?

The first invocation succeeds and prints the SVG path.

The identical second invocation, using the now-warm runtime transpiler cache, fails:

```text
SyntaxError: Missing 'default' export in module '/path/to/bun-runtime-cache-repro/asset.svg'.
```

Bun appears to parse the SVG as TSX on the cache-hit run instead of applying the built-in file loader.

### Additional information

This reproduces deterministically on:

- `1.4.0-canary.1+8adb8de8b`
- `1.4.0-canary.1+dc5748f36`
- `1.4.0-canary.1+aca54d5c2`
- Darwin arm64 and Linux x64

It was originally observed in a real `bun test` CI suite. With a fresh explicit cache, the test file passed all 26 tests on the first invocation. The identical second invocation failed while importing an SVG with the same missing-default-export error.

The likely cause is that the runtime-transpiler-cache hit returns before the main module sets `has_loaded`. Subsequent unknown-extension ESM imports therefore take the entry-point fallback and select the TSX loader instead of the `file` loader.

Segfault at 0xD0 in JSC GC parallel marking (SlotVisitor::visitChildren) — Bun 1.3.14, Linux arm64, long-running HTTP server

### What platform is your computer?

Crash report: https://bun.report/1.3.14/La10d9b296iC+gooCmw2wqE29D2suk9E2osk9E2o1k9E+q408Em7t/8Euvz/8E+1/wqEuzvhB2pv7BA2AgN

excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14+0d9b296af

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Bun reads `experimentalDecorators` / `emitDecoratorMetadata` from tsconfig when `extends` points at a relative path, but not when it points at a package specifier. Same config content, different result.

```sh
mkdir repro && cd repro
bun add reflect-metadata
mkdir -p node_modules/fake-tsconfig
cat > node_modules/fake-tsconfig/package.json <<'EOF'
{ "name": "fake-tsconfig", "version": "1.0.0" }
EOF
cat > node_modules/fake-tsconfig/flags.json <<'EOF'
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true
  }
}
EOF
cat > repro.ts <<'EOF'
import 'reflect-metadata';

function dec(target: unknown, key?: unknown) {
  console.log('decorator args:', typeof target, typeof key);
}
class Foo {
  @dec name!: string;
}
const meta = (Reflect as any).getMetadata?.('design:type', Foo.prototype, 'name');
console.log('design:type:', meta?.name ?? 'NOT EMITTED');
EOF
```

Case A, extends via package specifier:

```sh
echo '{ "extends": "fake-tsconfig/flags.json" }' > tsconfig.json
bun repro.ts
# decorator args: undefined object   <- TC39 decorator signature
# design:type: NOT EMITTED
```

Case B, identical file referenced by relative path:

```sh
cp node_modules/fake-tsconfig/flags.json ./flags.json
echo '{ "extends": "./flags.json" }' > tsconfig.json
bun repro.ts
# decorator args: object string      <- legacy decorator signature
# design:type: String

Case A behaves like case B: the extended config's `compilerOptions` apply, decorators compile with legacy semantics, and `design:*` metadata is emitted. That matches tsc's resolution of `extends` package specifiers (supported since TS 5.0) and bun's own handling of relative `extends`.

With the package-specifier form, the flags are silently ignored. Decorators get TC39 semantics and no metadata is emitted. There is no warning, so the failure shows up far from the cause.

title: node-compat: `new URL('/x#y', 'thismessage::/')` parses in node, throws in bun, and the jsonschema npm package depends on the node behavior
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14+0d9b296af

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```js
new URL('/x#y', 'thismessage::/');
// node 24.18.0 / 26.3.0: thismessage:/x#y
// bun 1.3.14: throws '"/x#y" cannot be parsed as a URL.'
```

The divergence is narrow. Here is the matrix (same script under both runtimes):

```
ref        base               node 24/26          bun 1.3.14
'/x#y'     'thismessage::/'   thismessage:/x#y    THROWS   <- the divergence
'/x'       'thismessage::/'   THROWS              THROWS
'x'        'thismessage::/'   THROWS              THROWS
'#y'       'thismessage::/'   thismessage::/#y    thismessage::/#y
'/x'       'thismessage:/'    thismessage:/x      thismessage:/x
'/x'       'a::/'             THROWS              THROWS
'/x'       'a:/b:/'           a:/x                a:/x
```

So both runtimes reject a path-absolute ref against an opaque-path base, which is what the WHATWG spec prescribes, except node makes an exception when the ref carries a fragment. Bun rejects that case too.

### What is the expected behavior?

Whatever node does, because npm packages depend on it. The `jsonschema` package's ref resolver does exactly this (https://github.com/tdegrunt/jsonschema/blob/master/lib/validator.js, in `Validator.prototype.resolve`):

```js
let parsed = new URL(switchSchema, 'thismessage::/');
```

with `switchSchema` values like `/undefined#/definitions/CommandMetaData`. On node that parses and only `parsed.hash` is consumed. On bun it throws, which in my case took down every CLI command of `@adonisjs/ace` (it validates command metadata through jsonschema).

### What do you see instead?

`"/x#y" cannot be parsed as a URL.`

### Additional information

Reading the URL standard, bun's rejection looks more spec-consistent than node's acceptance: a base with an opaque path should only accept empty or fragment-only relative refs, and node itself rejects `/x` without the fragment. The fragment exception looks like an Ada quirk. I am filing here first because bun's stated goal is node compatibility and this breaks published packages; happy to take it to Ada/node or jsonschema instead if you consider this a wontfix.

Workaround for anyone else hitting this through jsonschema: patch the base string to `'thismessage:/'` (single colon). Both runtimes parse that, and the resolver only reads `.hash` off the result, which is identical.

excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

The entire web and cloud-native ecosystem is betting heavily on WebAssembly (WASM). However, the Developer Experience (DX) for leveraging WASM in modern server-side JavaScript is severely broken and fragmented.

Currently, to achieve C-level performance, developers face two massive hurdles:

1. **Toolchain Hell**: They must leave JavaScript, write in a system language (Rust/Zig/C), install external toolchains (Cargo/Emscripten), manually compile `.wasm` binaries, and write tedious boilerplate to instantiate them via `WebAssembly.instantiate`. Even using AssemblyScript requires a separate build step and `asconfig.json`.
2. **The Memory Boundary (IPC) Bottleneck**: This is the fatal flaw. Passing complex data (like nested JSON or large arrays) from the JS heap to WASM's linear memory requires expensive serialization, copying, and deserialization (e.g., `TextEncoder` / `TextDecoder`). This memory boundary overhead often negates the performance gains of using WASM in the first place.

Bun is built on the philosophy of being an "All-in-One" toolkit. Forcing developers to rely on external build steps and manual memory copying to use WASM fundamentally breaks this philosophy.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

I propose a paradigm-shifting architecture: integrating a native TS-to-WASM compiler directly into the Bun runtime, featuring **Compiler-Magic Memory Sharing (Auto-Memory Hoisting)**.

By defining a specific block (e.g., `namespace Bun.InlineWasm`), developers can write a strictly-typed subset of TypeScript directly alongside their normal JS code in the *exact same file*.

Bun's compiler will hijack this block, bypass the JavaScriptCore engine, and AOT-compile the AST directly into WASM bytecode. More importantly, because Bun controls the compilation, it can perform **Auto-Memory Hoisting**: when a complex object is passed from the normal TS scope into the `InlineWasm` scope, Bun automatically allocates that object directly inside the WASM linear memory (or utilizes WasmGC), providing a transparent `Proxy` to the JS side.

title: ASAN CI: ExceptionScope::assertNoException during worker terminate (worker-transfer-terminate-stress, separate from #34095)
excerpt:
On the debian-13 x64-asan test lane, `test/js/node/worker_threads/worker-transfer-terminate-stress.test.ts` intermittently SIGABRTs with:

```
ASSERTION FAILED: (null)
!exception()
vendor/WebKit/Source/JavaScriptCore/runtime/ExceptionScope.h(61) : void JSC::ExceptionScope::assertNoException()
```

Observed on builds 75493, 75495, 75514, 75597, 75604, 75606 (6/6 hits are this signature). Release lanes are unaffected.

This is **not** the lazy-`PropertyCallback`-builder path tracked in #34095 (JSObject.cpp:3936 / JSCJSValuePropertyInlines.h:51). The vendored `test-worker-message-port-transfer-terminate.js` on the same lane hits JSObject.cpp:3936 almost exclusively (11 of 12 sampled builds); the stress test, which runs 8 rounds of 10 workers each, only ever hits ExceptionScope.h:61.

PR #33966 (the lazy-builder fix for #34095) reports in its Verification section:

> Under a 60-worker × 80-run bootstrap stress, a separate pre-existing `assertNoException()` at `ExceptionScope.h:61` still surfaces at about 1 in 4000 workers (termination landing later in the bootstrap, after the stdio builders have completed). That path is unrelated to the lazy-builder contract and not in scope here.

So this is a separate termination-vs-bootstrap race that survives the #33966/#33418 fixes. No symbolized backtrace is available from the CI annotations (the assertion aborts before the crash handler captures one).

Filing so the stress test's quarantine entry in `test/expectations.txt` has a tracker independent of #34095.

title: Feature: mmap the bytecode sidecar read-only so pooled processes share one copy
excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

PR #29291 (thanks!) makes ESM bytecode sidecars work without `--compile`, which makes bytecode usable for the pooled-worker pattern: a manager builds **one** artifact (`app.js` + `app.js.jsc`) and N long-lived worker processes each `import()` it.

In that shape, the sidecar's memory cost is paid N times. The loader reads the `.jsc` into a private heap buffer per process — nothing is mmap'd, so the kernel can't share pages across the pool, even though every process is reading the same immutable file.

**Measured** (macOS arm64, PR #29291 binary `1.4.0-canary.1+a4f165aef`; ~1.1 MB bundled ESM artifact with TLA + 5.3 MB `.jsc`; N long-lived processes each `await import(artifact)` then hold; medians over 3 rounds, variance ≈ 0):

| condition | phys_footprint / proc | aggregate (N procs) |
|---|---|---|
| bytecode, N=1 | 26.0 MB | 26.0 MB |
| bytecode, N=8 | 26.0 MB | 208.0 MB |
| plain, N=1 | 21.0 MB | 21.0 MB |
| plain, N=8 | 21.0 MB | 168.0 MB |

- Cost is perfectly linear: +5 MB phys_footprint per worker, ~the sidecar size, with zero cross-process sharing.
- `vmmap` confirms the mechanism: neither the artifact nor the `.jsc` appears as a mapped file in any worker (only ICU/tz/plist system files are mapped). The delta shows up as **private dirty anonymous memory** (`SM=PRV`): the allocator heap region (mimalloc — Bun's global allocator — tags its anonymous mappings with a VM tag that `vmmap` displays as `IOAccelerator`) carries 8256 KB dirty with bytecode vs 2896 KB plain — +5360 KB, almost exactly the 5330 KB sidecar, consistent with the sidecar bytes living in one owned heap allocation per process.
- Full raw data and methodology are in the two comments on the PR thread: [validation + timing](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/29291#issuecomment-5022315203) and [memory measurement](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/29291#issuecomment-5022639804).

robobun confirmed this reading at the source level on that thread:

> the sidecar path does a plain `File::read_from` into an owned buffer (the `.jsc` branch in `src/bundler/transpiler.rs`) and transfers ownership to JSC's `CachedBytecode`, so each process carries a private copy... Nothing in the current loader mmaps the artifact or the sidecar.

and suggested filing this as its own feature request, since it changes the `CachedBytecode` ownership model rather than the gate removed in #29291.

## Failure

`test/js/node/test/parallel/test-http2-reset-flood.js` intermittently dies with SIGABRT on the **debian 13 x64-asan** lane:

title: bun test swallows unhandled rejections from a script file's async IIFE
excerpt:
While running vendored Node tests (plain script files, no test() registrations) under `bun test --config=bunfig.node-test.toml`, an unhandled rejection inside the file's top-level async IIFE does not fail the run.

Concrete case: `test/js/node/test/parallel/test-child-process-advanced-serialization.js` has a deterministic assertion failure at line 41 (Buffer identity through advanced IPC), yet `bun test` reported the file as passing on every non-ASAN lane — only the ASAN lane surfaced it, via an unrelated abort. Running the same file directly (`bun <file>`) fails with the assertion as expected.

Impact: any vendored Node test whose body is an async IIFE can silently rot — CI green does not mean the assertions ran and held. This masked a real runtime gap for some time.

Expected: an unhandled rejection between/outside tests should fail the file, matching how uncaught exceptions between tests are already reported.

title: Advanced IPC and v8.serialize lose Buffer identity (no host-object hook in serializer)
excerpt:
`child_process` with `serialization: 'advanced'` and `v8.serialize/deserialize` round-trip `Buffer` values as plain `Uint8Array` — the prototype is lost.

Repro (advanced IPC): fork a child with `serialization: 'advanced'`, `cp.send({buffer: Buffer.from('Hello!')})`, echo it back: the received value's `buffer` is a `Uint8Array`, not a `Buffer`. Node preserves the Buffer via `ChildProcessSerializer._writeHostObject` (lib/internal/child_process/serialization.js).

Root cause: both paths go through JSC's `SerializedScriptValue`, which has no host-object hook, so there is no way to tag Buffer (or other typed-array subclasses) on the wire. A sound fix needs a serializer extension in the WebKit fork or a V8-wire-format serializer implementation.

Currently surfaced by vendored `test/js/node/test/parallel/test-child-process-advanced-serialization.js` (gated in expectations.txt on the branch that vendored it, citing this gap). Note the test's failure was itself masked on most lanes by the swallowed-rejection bug filed separately.

title: fs.writeFile does not flush on close when file is opened with O_APPEND, causing data loss on crash
excerpt:
## Summary

`Bun.fs.writeFile` does not flush pending writes to disk on close when the destination file is opened with `O_APPEND`. If the process crashes (or is killed) shortly after the write completes, the appended data is lost — it never reaches the kernel page cache in a durable state before the file descriptor is released.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open or create a file with `O_APPEND` (e.g. a log file that is repeatedly appended to).
2. Call `fs.writeFile(fd, data)` (or `fs.appendFile`) where `fd` was opened with `O_APPEND`.
3. Immediately after the promise resolves, kill the process (`kill -9`) or trigger a crash.
4. Reopen the file and inspect its contents.

```js
import { open, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const fh = await open("/tmp/append-test.log", "a"); // O_APPEND
await writeFile(fh, "this line should be durable after close\n");
// Simulate crash before next event loop tick:
process.kill(process.pid, "SIGKILL");
```

## Expected Behavior

On close, any buffered/queued writes for the `O_APPEND` descriptor should be flushed (via `fsync` or at minimum `fdatasync` before the descriptor is released). Data written before close should survive a crash that happens after the `writeFile` promise has resolved.

Node.js `fs.writeFile` / `fs.appendFile` flush on close for descriptors opened with `O_APPEND`, so appended data is durable once the promise resolves.

## Actual Behavior

On Bun, the `writeFile` promise resolves but the data is not flushed to disk before the descriptor is closed. A crash (or `SIGKILL`) that happens immediately after the promise resolves loses the appended data. The bytes never appear in the file after recovery.

## Environment

- Bun version: (please fill in — observed on latest stable as of report date)
- OS: Linux
- Platform: x86_64

## Additional Context

This manifests most visibly for log files opened once with `O_APPEND` and written to repeatedly. The close path appears to skip the flush that Node performs, so any in-flight pages are dropped on crash rather than being written back before the descriptor is released.

A `git bisect` was not performed; the behavior appears to be longstanding rather than a regression in a specific release.

title: Segfault in JSC MicrotaskQueue::drain (generator microtasks) on rapid PTY shrink — macOS aarch64, Bun 1.3.14 standalone
excerpt:
**What happened**
opencode 1.18.4 (a Bun 1.3.14 standalone executable, NAPI module loaded) segfaults when its
host terminal is rapidly resized down to extreme sizes (~2 cols × 1 row). The crash is inside
the VM's microtask machinery, not application JS — the VM should surface a catchable error
(e.g. RangeError on stack exhaustion) rather than segfault.

**Crash reports (two independent hits, same stack family)**
- https://bun.report/1.3.14/Ma10d9b296mwGugogC________urh5kDunr21Cusw11C+/y34C+qy34C+5sy6Cu657H__urh5kD27p5tC+xt2yCA2K4/vshtD
- https://bun.report/1.3.14/Ma10d9b296mwGugogC_______2lkjlDurh5kDunr21Cusw11C+/y34C+qy34C+5sy6Cu657H__urh5kD27p5tC+xt2yCA2K4/ny3zD

Decoded (first report): `Segmentation fault at 0x5084EEFFC` —
`llint_call_javascript` → `MicrotaskCall::tryCallWithArguments<JSGenerator…>` →
`callMicrotask` (JSMicrotask.cpp:143) → `runInternalMicrotask` → `MicrotaskQueue::drainImpl<true>`
→ `VM::drainMicrotasks` → `Bun::jsFunctionDrainMicrotaskQueue` (BunProcess.cpp:3806).
Features: spawn, standalone_executable, workers_spawned, napi_module_register, process_dlopen.

**Environment**
macOS 15 (Darwin 25.4.0), Apple Silicon. The terminal host is xterm.js inside a Tauri app
(PTY via portable-pty); the process group receives SIGWINCH + TIOCSWINSZ per resize step,
~10–120 ms apart, down to 2×1. Process RSS was ~1.0 GB at the time (this instance's normal
baseline in that workspace — not a leak ramp).

**Reproduction honesty**
Hit twice in the real app (both reports above). We could NOT isolate a standalone repro:
headless PTY harnesses (single jump to 1×1, 1-col staircase drags at 20–100 ms cadence with
bounces, floor jitter, DSR/XTWINOPS query replies, SGR mouse-motion floods with out-of-range
coordinates) all survive. Whatever the missing ingredient is, it's timing/state-dependent in
the real xterm.js byte stream. Happy to run instrumented builds or gather more data.

**Downstream mitigation (for anyone else hitting this)**
Host-side: never report a grid below 20×5 to the PTY (real terminals have window minimums;
after flooring, the crash class is unreachable). Implemented in our terminal host.

### What is the problem this feature would solve?

## Description

Bun is becoming a full-stack JavaScript/TypeScript runtime, but currently developers still need third-party libraries such as `systeminformation` to access basic system information.

I would like to propose adding a built-in system information API to Bun, providing a fast, lightweight, and modern alternative implemented natively in Rust.

## Motivation

Many backend applications, CLI tools, monitoring services, and developer tools need access to system information, for example:

- CPU information

title: node:tls: NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 disables the default requestCert enforcement on tls.Server / http2.createSecureServer
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1+5b98630ac (also present on current main, e550f2c36a)

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

`tls.createServer({ requestCert: true })` with `rejectUnauthorized` left unset is supposed to default to `true` and reject clients whose certificate can't be verified — that's what PR #31322 fixed. The default is computed by `rejectUnauthorizedDefault()` in `src/js/node/tls.ts`, which reads `process.env.NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED`. That env var is only supposed to affect the client side (whether you accept a remote server's cert when connecting out). On real Node.js it has no effect on a server's own client-cert enforcement. On Bun it does, because the server default and the client default both go through the same function.

So if anything in the process sets `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` — a very common one-liner people add to work around a self-signed cert on some unrelated outbound `fetch`/`https.request` call — every `tls.createServer`/`http2.createSecureServer` with mTLS silently stops enforcing it, without the server code ever touching `rejectUnauthorized`.

title: [Bug] Bun Windows - Stale process.env values from transpilation cache
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1+5b98630ac

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19044.0 x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Create a single file `index.ts`:
```ts
console.log("HOST:", process.env.DATABASE_HOST);
```

2. Create `.env`:
```env
DATABASE_HOST="value-A"
```

3. Run it (establishes transpilation cache):
```
$ bun index.ts
HOST: value-A
```

4. Change `.env` **without modifying any `.ts` file**:
```env
DATABASE_HOST="value-B"
```

5. Run again:
```
$ bun index.ts
HOST: value-A
```

The output is **still `value-A`** even though `.env` says `value-B`.

6. Even deleting `.env` entirely and running again **still prints `value-A`**, proving the value comes from a cached transpilation, not from the filesystem.

7. The only fix: modify any byte of `index.ts` (add a comment, then remove it), which forces re-transpilation and picks up the new `.env` value.

### What is the expected behavior?

Each `bun index.ts` invocation starts a fresh process, reads `.env` from disk, and all `process.env.*` accesses happen at runtime. Changing `.env` should take effect on the next run.

### What do you see instead?

`process.env.*` values are permanently baked into a transpilation cache keyed by **source file content hash**. Changing `.env` does not invalidate the cache. The application silently uses stale values with no warning or error.

Evidence table:

| Step | `.env` value | Source file changed? | Output |
|------|-------------|---------------------|--------|
| 1 | `value-A` | No (original) | `value-A` (establishes cache) |
| 2 | `value-B` | No | `value-A` (stale from cache) |
| 3 | `.env` deleted entirely | No | `value-A` (proves cache, not `.env`) |
| 4 | `value-C` | Yes (added a comment) | `value-C` (cache invalidated) |
| 5 | `value-A` | Reverted to original | `value-A` (old cache hit again) |

### Additional information

- **Windows-specific** - the same files under Docker Linux (`oven/bun:canary-slim`) correctly pick up new `.env` values every run.
- The transpilation cache lives in `%TEMP%\bun-*`. Deleting these directories clears the stale cache (but affects all Bun projects).
- **Workaround**: touch every `.ts` file that reads `process.env` after any `.env` change to force re-transpilation.
- Any `process.env` access is affected; `import { SQL } from 'bun'` in the original project was coincidental.

title: Bun.build: external ["node:zlib"] not honored when minify is enabled — polyfill bundled instead
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14 (0d9b296a) — macOS arm64

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.x arm64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

`entry.ts`:

```ts
export async function go(data: Uint8Array): Promise<Uint8Array> {
  const { deflateSync } = await import("node:zlib");
  return new Uint8Array(deflateSync(data));
}
```

`build.ts`:

```ts
await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ["entry.ts"],
  outdir: "out",
  format: "esm",
  target: "browser",
  minify: true,
  external: ["node:zlib"],
});
```

### What is the expected behavior?

The `await import("node:zlib")` stays a runtime import in the output — which is exactly what happens when `minify` is omitted: `grep -c "node:zlib" out/entry.js` reports 1, and no zlib implementation is bundled.

### What do you see instead?

With `minify: true`, the external import is replaced by Bun's bundled node:zlib browser polyfill: output grows from ~1 KB to ~260 KB (minified), and `node:zlib` no longer appears in the output at all. The externalization is silently dropped.

Granular isolation:

- `minify: { whitespace: true }` → polyfill bundled, external broken
- `minify: { identifiers: true }` → external honored
- `minify: { syntax: true }` → external honored
- `external: ["node:zlib", "zlib"]` and wildcard variants → still broken under minify

So the whitespace minifier specifically causes the external `node:` builtin to be replaced by the polyfill.

### Additional information

Real-world impact: migrating a production esbuild build (`--minify --external:node:zlib`, 12 entry points) to Bun.build. The polyfill adds ~290–350 KB per affected bundle and changes a deliberate dual-environment fallback (`CompressionStream` in browsers, `node:zlib` elsewhere) — blocking the migration until externalization survives minification.

title: Bun.listen: NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 disables the default requestCert enforcement (same gap as #33754, missed by #33755's tests)
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1+5b98630ac (repo checked out at feee846272, current main as of this report)

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is the native `Bun.listen()`/`Bun.connect()` version of the `node:tls` bug in #35092, and it's related to #33754 (`Bun.listen()` does not enforce `rejectUnauthorized`, fixed by #33755), but it's a different, still-open gap in the same area.

`Bun.listen({ tls: { requestCert: true } })` with `rejectUnauthorized` left unset is supposed to default to `true`, same as `requestCert`'s documented behavior everywhere else in Bun. The default is computed in `src/runtime/socket/SSLConfig.rs`:

```rust
result.reject_unauthorized = generated
    .reject_unauthorized
    .unwrap_or_else(|| vm.get_tls_reject_unauthorized())
    as i32;
```

`vm.get_tls_reject_unauthorized()` reads `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED`. This function builds the SSL config for both `Bun.listen` (server) and `Bun.connect` (client) - it has no `is_server` parameter, so it can't tell which role it's defaulting for. `resolve_reject_unauthorized()` (added by #33755, same file) then uses that value directly for the server's enforcement decision:

```rust
Some(cfg) => (!is_server || cfg.request_cert != 0) && cfg.reject_unauthorized != 0,
```

So a server with `requestCert: true` and no explicit `rejectUnauthorized` enforces correctly only as long as nothing in the process has set `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` - a very common one-liner for working around a self-signed cert on some unrelated outbound request.

Repro (self-signed test certs generated locally with openssl, 10-year validity; server's CA store is a third, unrelated self-signed cert - non-empty, but it doesn't trust the client's cert - so the rejection can't be explained by an empty trust store):

```js

const key = `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----

process.binding("http_parser").methods contains "M - SEARCH" instead of "M-SEARCH"
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

Verified on 1.3.14, and the root cause is still present on `main`.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```js
const { methods, allMethods } = process.binding("http_parser");
console.log(methods.includes("M-SEARCH"));   // false
console.log(methods.includes("M - SEARCH")); // true  ← note the spaces
```

### What is the expected behavior?

`process.binding("http_parser").methods` (and `allMethods`) should contain the HTTP method token `"M-SEARCH"`, matching:

- the public `require("node:http").METHODS`, which is correct (`"M-SEARCH"`),
- Node's `process.binding("http_parser").methods`,
- the IANA/SSDP method token `M-SEARCH` (UPnP discovery).

### What do you see instead?

The list contains the malformed `"M - SEARCH"` (spaces around the hyphen) instead of `"M-SEARCH"`. Every other method matches Node.

### Root cause

`src/jsc/bindings/node/http/llhttp/llhttp.h` (lines 356 and 409) has:

```c
XX(24, MSEARCH, M - SEARCH)      \
```

Upstream llhttp (this file is vendored llhttp v9.3.0) defines it as `XX(24, M_SEARCH, M-SEARCH)`. The extra spaces — most likely introduced by a `clang-format` pass treating `-` as a binary operator in the vendored macro table — get stringized by the C preprocessor into `"M - SEARCH"`, which then flows into `llhttp_method_name(24)` and out through the `process.binding("http_parser")` compat layer.

`M-SEARCH` is the only hyphenated method in the table, so it's the only entry affected.

### Suggested fix

- In `llhttp.h`, restore `M - SEARCH` → `M-SEARCH` on both lines (and, since this is vendored, consider excluding `src/jsc/bindings/node/http/llhttp/` from clang-format so it can't recur).
- `packages/bun-types/overrides.d.ts` (lines 266 and 303) currently mirrors the typo in the `methods`/`allMethods` literal types — those `"M - SEARCH"` literals should be corrected to `"M-SEARCH"` in the same change so the types match the fixed runtime.

Bun's own HTTP server method handling (`src/http_types/Method.rs`) already uses the correct `"M-SEARCH"`, so this is limited to the `process.binding("http_parser")` / node:http compat surface — but it's still a wrong method token there.

title: `http.Server` cannot adopt external sockets via `emit('connection')`
excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

In latest bun canary there is massively improved support for `new tls.TLSSocket` which works great - thanks. This has almost unblocked our ability to run a node application on Bun, but there's one blocker remaining.

Node's `http.Server` has an internal `connectionListener` that attaches an
`HTTPParser` to every socket passed through the `connection` event. This
allows user code to feed arbitrary Duplex streams (e.g. a TLS-terminated
socket from a proxy) into `http.createServer()` by calling
`server.emit('connection', socket)`.

Bun's `http.Server` does not have a JS-side connection listener. HTTP
parsing is done natively by uWS, and uWS only parses sockets that the
server itself accepted via `listen()`. Calling `emit('connection', socket)`
registers no parser on the socket — `request` events never fire.

Here is a reproduction: 

[bun-repro-emit-connection.js](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30307977/bun-repro-emit-connection.js)


### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Bun's `http.Server` (in `_http_server.ts`) registers no JS-side listener
for the `connection` event. Connections are instead delivered via the
native `onServerConnection` callback — uWS calls this directly when a
TCP connection arrives on the listening socket. The internal HTTP parser
and response pipeline are wired to the native uWS handle, not to an
abstract Duplex interface.

In Node, `_http_server.js` does:

```js
this.on('connection', connectionListener);
```

Where `connectionListener` attaches an `HTTPParser` to the socket,
wires `socket.on('data', …)` → parser, and emits `request` when a
complete HTTP message is parsed. Any Duplex passed through the
`connection` event gets parsed.


### What alternatives have you considered?

A workaround is to listen the http.Server on an ephemeral loopback port and pipe the decrypted stream through a `net.connect()` bridge — an extra TCP connection per tunnel.

excerpt:
**ROOT CAUSE CORRECTION** (deep-dived on `main` @ `892b1dab` — the original analysis below is preserved but its mechanism was wrong):

The panic is **not** about signal delivery during streaming at all. It is:

## `Bun.Subprocess.kill(signalName)` maps signal names with the LINUX signal-number table on macOS

`src/bun_core/Global.rs` — the canonical `for_each_signal!` X-macro that generates `SignalCode` — hardcodes Linux numbers unconditionally:

```rust
SIGBUS = 7, SIGFPE = 8, SIGKILL = 9, SIGUSR1 = 10, SIGSEGV = 11, SIGUSR2 = 12, ...
SIGCHLD = 17, SIGCONT = 18, SIGSTOP = 19, SIGTSTP = 20, ... SIGIO = 29, SIGPWR = 30, SIGSYS = 31
```

On Darwin (`<sys/signal.h>`): `SIGUSR1=30`, `SIGUSR2=31`, `SIGBUS=10`, `SIGSYS=12`, `SIGURG=16`, `SIGSTOP=17`, `SIGTSTP=18`, `SIGCONT=19`, `SIGCHLD=20`, `SIGIO=23`, `SIGINFO=29`, `SIGEMT=7` — everything outside 1–6, 8, 9, 11, 13–15, 21–22, 24–28 diverges.

`subprocess.kill("SIGUSR1")` → `FromJsEnum for bun_sys::SignalCode` (`src/jsc/lib.rs`) → `signal_code::from_name` → **10** → `kill(child, 10)` = **SIGBUS on macOS**. Bun's crash reporter in the child catches the externally-sent SIGBUS with `si_addr = 0` and prints `panic: Bus error at address 0x0` — which is exactly the "panic" in my original report. The child's JS `SIGUSR1` handler "never ran" because SIGUSR1 was never sent. The streaming response was a red herring (it merely made the child a Bun process someone wanted to signal gracefully).

### Discriminating evidence (macOS 15.7.7 arm64, reproduces on 1.3.14 stable AND 1.4.0 canary `2892b1da`)

A bash child that traps everything, signalled each way:

```
Subprocess.kill("SIGUSR1")     → child saw: GOT-BUS     ← Linux 10 = macOS SIGBUS
Subprocess.kill("SIGUSR2")     → child saw: GOT-SYS     ← Linux 12 = macOS SIGSYS
Subprocess.kill(30)            → child saw: GOT-USR1    ← numeric passes through correctly
Subprocess.kill("SIGTERM")     → child saw: GOT-TERM    ← 15 on both platforms, works
process.kill(pid, "SIGUSR1")   → child saw: GOT-USR1    ← process.kill maps correctly (separate path)
node:child_process .kill("SIGUSR1") → GOT-USR1          ← node-compat maps correctly (separate path)
```

And shell `kill -USR1 <bun pid>` is handled perfectly fine by `process.on("SIGUSR1")` even mid-stream — confirming signal *delivery* was never the bug.

### Reverse direction is broken by the same table

A child killed by a **real** SIGUSR1 (`/bin/kill -30`) is reported as:

```js
proc.signalCode === "SIGPWR"   // Linux name for 3

title: Bun.Image should support TIFF decoding on Linux
excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

`Bun.Image` can identify TIFF input, but decoding TIFF is unsupported on Linux and returns `ERR_IMAGE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED`. The same API relies on native platform image backends on macOS and Windows, so behavior differs by deployment platform.

This prevents Linux server and Lambda applications that accept TIFF uploads from fully replacing Sharp. In my project, TIFF decoding is the only reason a Sharp/libvips fallback remains after migrating the rest of the image pipeline to `Bun.Image`.

The limitation is documented in Bun's [platform backend table](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/image#platform-backends), but TIFF is already represented as an image format and detected by the runtime. A Linux decoder would make the API portable for this input format.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Add decode-only TIFF support to `Bun.Image` on Linux.

A portable TIFF decoder could feed Bun's existing decoded-pixel pipeline when no native Linux backend is available. Supporting the first image/page and normalizing it to Bun's existing RGBA8 representation would cover the common server-side ingestion case; TIFF encoding is not needed for this request.

Ideally this would work on the Linux targets commonly used for Bun deployments and Lambdas, including x64/arm64 and glibc/musl, while enforcing `maxPixels` before allocating the decoded output.

### What alternatives have you considered?

- Keep Sharp/libvips solely as a TIFF-to-PNG fallback. This works, but retains a large native dependency and its Lambda packaging/build complexity for one input format.
- Reject TIFF uploads on Linux. This would regress an existing supported upload path.
- Convert TIFF files in a separate service or external binary. This adds operational complexity and another runtime boundary for a conversion that otherwise belongs in the image pipeline.

title: Bun.Image: add `fastShrinkOnLoad: false` for quality-first JPEG resizing
excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

`Bun.Image` currently always applies aggressive JPEG IDCT shrink-on-load when a pipeline contains a downscale: it selects the smallest libjpeg-turbo M/8 decode size that is still at least the final target, then runs the requested resize filter. This is fast, but there is no quality-first opt-out.

We run a production photo pipeline that generates smart-cropped cards and squares, true-aspect srcset rungs, social previews, and avatars from user uploads. Sharp exposes `fastShrinkOnLoad: false` specifically for this tradeoff. Its conservative path can still use JPEG shrink-on-load, but leaves at least 2× target resolution for the final Lanczos resize, avoiding the slight moiré and excess sharpness that the aggressive path can introduce.

We measured the two Sharp modes on six representative production JPEGs. Enabling `fastShrinkOnLoad` made draft-ready variant generation only 0.9% faster, while average SSIMULACRA2 versus our current quality-first resize reference dropped by 2.10 points. One difficult `square640` crop fell from 73.05 to 37.35. For a permanent delivery-variant pipeline, that quality loss is not worth the negligible CPU saving.

This is a remaining blocker for replacing Sharp in the production pipeline described in #32122.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Add a Sharp-compatible resize option:

```ts
await new Bun.Image(input)
  .resize(1920, 1920, {
    fit: "inside",
    withoutEnlargement: true,
    fastShrinkOnLoad: false,
  })
  .webp({ quality: 90 })
  .bytes();
```

Proposed semantics:

- `fastShrinkOnLoad: true` remains the default and preserves Bun's current behavior.
- For JPEG input, `false` chooses a conservative libjpeg IDCT scaling factor that leaves at least 2× target resolution on the limiting axis for the final resize kernel, matching Sharp's quality-first behavior.
- This does not need to disable IDCT shrink-on-load completely; the important contract is retaining enough intermediate resolution for a consistent final resample.
- For formats where Bun does not perform decoder-side scaling, the option can be a no-op.

Keeping the current default avoids any performance regression for existing users while allowing image pipelines to choose output quality explicitly.

### What alternatives have you considered?

- Keep Sharp only for resizing. This preserves quality but prevents replacing the native addon and libvips/jemalloc operational stack with `Bun.

title: Fatal uncaught exception runs already-queued fs callbacks before exiting (node exits immediately)
excerpt:
🤖 Found while reviewing #34661's callback-guard work; pre-existing (reproduces on released bun), filed for tracking per review policy.

With no `uncaughtException` handler installed, a fatal throw should terminate the process before any other queued work runs — node exits immediately. Bun drains already-queued fs completion callbacks during VM teardown first, so user code observably runs after the fatal error.

**Repro** (identical on released bun and current branches):

```js
const fs = require("fs");
fs.stat(".", () => console.log("fs callback ran"));
process.nextTick(() => { throw new Error("fatal"); });
```

- node v26.3.0: prints the uncaught error, exit 1, **no** `fs callback ran`
- bun: prints `fs callback ran`, then exit 1

The divergence is user-visible side effects: a callback that writes files, sends network data, or mutates state runs in bun where node guarantees it never does. Class: VM teardown ordering — the fatal-error path should stop the event loop before draining pending native completions, not after.

Not specific to fs — any already-queued libuv completion appears to behave the same. #34661 reroutes callback *throws* onto the uncaught path (matching node) but does not change this exit-ordering; the two are independent.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

A `u32`/`uint32_t` FFI argument whose JS value is above `2^31` (so stored as a double, not an Int32) reaches C as the wrong value on Windows. Values below `2^31` are correct.

```c
// clang -shared -O2 -o lib.dll lib.c
#include <stdint.h>
__declspec(dllexport) uint32_t echo_u32(uint32_t v) { return v; }
```

```js
import { dlopen } from "bun:ffi";
const { symbols: { echo_u32 } } = dlopen("./lib.dll", {
  echo_u32: { args: ["u32"], returns: "u32" },
});
console.log(echo_u32(3000000000)); // prints 3221225472 (0xC0000000), expected 3000000000
console.log(echo_u32(12345));      // prints 12345 (correct)
```

The `run ffi > integer identities > uint32_t` test in `test/js/bun/ffi/ffi.test.js` hits this as `expected 2147483648, received -2147483648` (return value interpreted as signed), but the test is skipped on Windows CI because no compiled `bun-ffi-test.dll` is present.

### What is the expected behavior?

`3000000000`

### What do you see instead?

`3221225472` (`0xC0000000`). The double → u32 conversion in the TinyCC-generated trampoline is producing garbage for out-of-int32-range inputs on Windows.

Does **not** reproduce on the JSC-native FFI path in #35246 (that path returns `3000000000` correctly), so this will be fixed once that lands; filing so it's tracked in case the kill switch needs to stay usable on Windows.

The project depends on ~16 packages that are all **branches of one private git repository**

bun install rewrites `resolved` of already-locked packages to the configured registry, making bun.lock non-portable
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin arm64 (also observed on Linux and macOS CI runners)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

When a registry is configured that does **not** rewrite `dist.tarball` to its own host — a transparent proxy, as opposed to a mirror like `registry.npmmirror.com` — an install that updates the lockfile rewrites the `resolved` field of every **already-locked** package to an absolute URL on that registry. Newly added packages correctly keep `""`.

```sh
mkdir demo && cd demo
echo '{"name":"demo","private":true,"dependencies":{"is-odd":"3.0.1"}}' > package.json

# 1. Baseline against the default registry
printf 'registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/\n' > .npmrc
bun install

# 2. Add one dependency while a transparent-proxy registry is configured
printf 'registry=https://npm.flatt.tech/\n' > .npmrc          # serves anonymously
echo '{"name":"demo","private":true,"dependencies":{"is-odd":"3.0.1","is-even":"1.0.0"}}' > package.json
bun install
```

### What is the expected behavior?

`bun.lock` stays registry-agnostic, as it is when installing against the default registry or against a mirror that rewrites `dist.tarball` (`registry.npmmirror.com` produces no URLs at all in the same test).

### What do you see instead?

Step 1:

```
"is-number": ["is-number@6.0.0", ""
"is-odd":    ["is-odd@3.0.1",    ""
```

Step 2 — the newly added package is fine, but the two pre-existing entries were rewritten:

```
"is-even":   ["is-even@1.0.0",   ""
"is-number": ["is-number@6.0.0", "https://npm.flatt.tech/is-number/-/is-number-6.0.0.tgz"
"is-odd":    ["is-odd@3.0.1",    "https://npm.flatt.tech/is-odd/-/is-odd-3.0.1.tgz"
```

### Additional information

The trigger appears to be a mismatch between the configured registry and the tarball host in the package metadata:

| registry | `dist.tarball` for `is-odd@3.0.1` | `resolved` written |
|---|---|---|
| `registry.npmjs.org` | `https://registry.npmjs.org/...` | `""` |
| `registry.npmmirror.com` | `https://registry.npmmirror.com/...` | `""` |
| `npm.flatt.tech` (transparent proxy) | `https://registry.npmjs.org/...` | absolute URL **on the proxy host** |

Note the third row rewrites to the *configured registry's* host rather than to the `dist.tarball` value.

Why this matters in practice: `bun.lock` is committed and shared. A CI job that routes installs through a proxy and commits an updated lockfile silently pins the whole dependency graph to that proxy

### What platform is your computer?

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is a follow-up to #34437, which was closed after a debug-build verification that did not demonstrate an actual cache restoration.

Run:

```sh
mkdir bun-runtime-cache-repro
cd bun-runtime-cache-repro

printf '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"/>' > asset.svg

# read and then intentionally discard restored transpiler-cache entries.

bun run run.ts
bun run run.ts
```

The entry point must be larger than the runtime transpiler cache's 4 KiB minimum. The first invocation writes the cache entry; the second invocation restores it.

`BUN_DEBUG_ENABLE_RESTORE_FROM_TRANSPILER_CACHE=1` is harmless on release builds and ensures that debug-build verification exercises the actual cache-hit path.

The first invocation succeeds:

```text

```text
SyntaxError: Missing 'default' export in module '/path/to/bun-runtime-cache-repro/asset.svg'.

Disabling the cache with `BUN_RUNTIME_TRANSPILER_CACHE_PATH=0` makes repeated invocations succeed.

excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14+0d9b296af

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

`path.win32.normalize` and `path.win32.join` skip two guards that Node applies, so a relative path that would come back looking like a drive or a DOS device is returned as-is instead of being prefixed with `.\`.

In Node's `lib/path.js`, `win32.normalize` returns `` `.\\${tail}` `` when the input is relative, no device was resolved, and the tail would otherwise start with a drive specifier or contain a colon at the end of a segment. The comment above that branch cites CVE-2024-36139. Separately, `win32.join` skips normalization entirely when any part is a reserved DOS name, which leaves `..` uncollapsed on purpose.

```js
import path from "node:path";
const p = path.win32;
const B = String.fromCharCode(92);
const q = s => JSON.stringify(s);

console.log(q(p.normalize("CON:")));
console.log(q(p.normalize("uploads/../CON:")));
console.log(q(p.normalize("uploads/../c:")));
console.log(q(p.normalize("a/../../c:")));
console.log(q(p.normalize("a" + B + "c:")));
console.log(q(p.join("uploads", "c:")));
console.log(q(p.join("uploads", "..", "c:")));
console.log(q(p.join("uploads", ".." + B + "CON:")));
console.log(q(p.join("a", "b", "c:")));
```

### What is the expected behavior?

Node v24.16.0:

```
normalize("CON:")                 ".\\CON:."
normalize("uploads/../CON:")      ".\\CON:"
normalize("uploads/../c:")        ".\\c:"
normalize("a/../../c:")           ".\\..\\c:"
normalize("a\\c:")                ".\\a\\c:"
join("uploads", "c:")             ".\\uploads\\c:"
join("uploads", "..", "c:")       ".\\c:"
join("uploads", "..\\CON:")       "uploads\\..\\CON:"
join("a", "b", "c:")              ".\\a\\b\\c:"
```

### What do you see instead?

Bun 1.3.14:

```
normalize("CON:")                 "CON:"
normalize("uploads/../CON:")      "CON:"
normalize("uploads/../c:")        "c:"
normalize("a/../../c:")           "..\\c:"
normalize("a\\c:")                "a\\c:"

join("uploads", "..", "c:")       "c:"
join("uploads", "..\\CON:")       "CON:"
join("a", "b", "c:")              "a\\b\\c:"

title: bun test: panic on a single positional argument >= 997 bytes (fixed 1023-byte buffer)
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1 (892b1dabc)

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.2, Apple Silicon (arm64)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

`bun test` panics when **a single positional argument** is 997 bytes or longer. The path does not need to exist and no repo state is required:

```sh
# 997-byte argument -> panic
bun test "$(python3 -c "print('./x' + 'a'*986 + '.test.ts')")"
```

Output:

```
bun test v1.4.0-canary.1 (892b1dabc)

panic: range end index 1024 out of range for slice of length 1023
oh no: Bun has crashed. This indicates a bug in Bun, not your code.
```

One byte shorter is fine:

```sh
# 996-byte argument -> no panic
bun test "$(python3 -c "print('./x' + 'a'*985 + '.test.ts')")"
```

### What is the expected behavior?

An over-long positional should be treated as a filter that matches nothing — which is exactly how a short non-existent path already behaves — or produce a normal error. Not a panic.

```sh
bun test ./nope.ts          # no panic, behaves sensibly
```

### What do you see instead?

A panic. Bisected results, in case they help locate the buffer:

| argument length | result |
|---|---|
| 996 | ok |
| 997 | `panic: range end index 1024 out of range for slice of length 1023` |
| 998 | `panic: range end index 1025 …` |
| 999 | `panic: range end index 1026 …` |
| 1000 | `panic: range end index 1027 …` |
| 1023 | `panic: range end index 1050 …` |
| 1024 | `panic: range end index 1051 …` |

The reported end index is consistently **`argument length + 27`**, and the slice length is always **1023**. That looks like a fixed 1023-byte buffer being written with a ~27-byte prefix and no bounds check — the panic begins at exactly the length where `len + 27` first exceeds 1023.

Two things that are *not* required:

**It is per-argument, not total argv length.** 120 short positionals totalling 1570 bytes are fine:

```sh
bun test ./x0.test.ts ./x1.test.ts … ./x119.test.ts    # 1570 bytes total, no panic
```

**`--parallel` is not involved.** It panics identically with and without it.

### Additional information

We hit this from tooling rather than by hand. A test runner that narrows a suite to a changed-file subset builds a list of paths; if that list gets joined into a single shell word instead of being passed as separate argv entries, it crosses 997 bytes at roughly a dozen paths and the run dies with a panic instead of an error. ### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

There is no code snippet. The trigger is external to the JavaScript being executed: another process on the system injects into the Bun process and faults it. I have a deterministic environmental reproduction instead, which works in both directions.

Setup

On Windows, install Claude Code via the native installer (ships a Bun 1.4.0 standalone executable).
Install Helldivers 2 (Steam). It loads nProtect GameGuard, a process-scanning anti-cheat that injects into other processes.

Reproduction A — game starts second

Start an interactive Claude Code session and leave it running.
Launch Helldivers 2 and enter gameplay.
Segfault. In my case after roughly 80 minutes of session uptime.

Reproduction B — game starts first (faster, use this one)

Launch Helldivers 2 first.
Start Claude Code.
Segfault in about 2 seconds.

Reproduction B is the practical one: 2,182 ms from launch to crash. Neither reproduces with the game closed.

Minimal version, for anyone able to test without Claude Code: run any Bun process that exercises the JIT while GameGuard is active. I have not isolated a smaller reproducer and do not have a standalone Bun install on this machine to try.

### What is the expected behavior?

The Bun process continues running. Another application starting on the same machine should not terminate it.

Failing that: if a memory allocation or page-protection call is blocked by an external hook, Bun should detect the null return and surface a diagnostic identifying the failed operation, rather than dereferencing it and faulting. A message naming the failed call would let affected users identify the cause themselves. At present the crash is indistinguishable from any other segfault, which is likely why this trigger has gone unidentified across a number of similar reports.

title: [Build] bun's very intrusive build.ts constantly enforced -march=haswell is hardcoded and overrides CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS, breaking cross-compilation for older CPUs
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.3.14

### What platform is your computer?

debian trixie liunx 6.12.96-rt-amd64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Attempting to build Bun from source for a specific CPU architecture (e.g., Westmere) is currently impossible without patching and locking the local git repo CMake files, due to build.ts always reverting/enforcing the architecture to "Haswell" in the cmake files, even after just patching!

Bun's CMakeLists.txt and cmake/CompilerFlags.cmake hardcode -march=haswell. Because of CMake's flag ordering, this hardcoded flag is appended after my custom CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS. Since Clang obeys the last -march flag it sees, the target architecture is completely ignored.

Furthermore, if LTO is enabled, this hardcoded Haswell flag poisons the LTO bitcode, causing the final bun-profile binary to crash with an Illegal instruction (SIGILL) when executed on a non-Haswell CPU.

Steps to Reproduce:

    On a machine with a CPU older than Haswell (e.g., Westmere), clone Bun.
    Set CC=clang, CXX=clang++, and CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS to -march=westmere.
    Run bun run build:release.
    The build will compile, but during the final link step, -march=haswell is injected. 
    When CMake tries to run bun-profile --revision at the end of the build, it crashes with Illegal instruction.


### What is the expected behavior?

Provided CFLAGS and CXXFLAGS (or at least a CMake variable like -DZIG_TARGET_ARCH=westmere) should take precedence over hardcoded defaults, allowing users to build optimized binaries for their specific CPU architecture without manually patching .cmake files.

### What do you see instead?

Corrupted binaries, due to persistent poisoning of the build cmake files.

### Additional information

Environment:

     OS: Debian Trixie
     Clang: 21 (also tested with 22)
     CPU: Intel Westmerefter

title: Feature Request: Native Bindings for Server, Request, and Response in Bun Native Plugins
excerpt:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

# Feature Request: Native Bindings for `Server`, `Request`, and `Response` in Bun Native Plugins

First of all, thank you for the incredible work on Bun. The performance improvements in recent releases, especially the ongoing Rust work, have made Bun an excellent platform for building high-performance server frameworks.

I'm currently developing **Ingress**, a framework built specifically **on top of Bun**, not as a replacement for it. Bun handles networking and the HTTP runtime exceptionally well, while Ingress focuses on reducing application-layer overhead through native processing.

## Current Limitation

Today, native plugins (NAPI or future native plugin APIs) have limited access to Bun's internal HTTP primitives.

Because of this, a framework that wants to perform request processing natively has to repeatedly bridge between JavaScript and Rust or reconstruct data that Bun has already parsed.

For example, tasks such as:

* request parsing
* query parsing
* header parsing
* cookie parsing
* DTO validation
* request sanitization
* security checks
* context construction

can all be executed efficiently in Rust before the application handler runs.

However, without native access to Bun's HTTP objects, some of these optimizations require unnecessary conversions or additional work at the JS/native boundary.

## Feature Proposal

It would be extremely useful if Bun exposed native bindings (or another stable native interface) for:

* `Server`
* `Request`
* `Response`

The goal would **not** be to replace Bun's HTTP implementation, but to allow native extensions to build directly on top of Bun's existing infrastructure.

For example, a native plugin could:

* access request metadata without recreating JS objects
* read headers and URL components directly
* expose zero-copy views where possible
* create or modify responses natively
* interact with Bun's request lifecycle without unnecessary conversions

## Potential API Direction

I'm not suggesting a specific implementation, but something conceptually similar to:

```rust
struct NativeRequest {
    // access to Bun's parsed request
}

struct NativeResponse {
    // construct or modify response
}

struct NativeServer {
    // lifecycle hooks
}
```

or another API that exposes these capabilities while maintaining Bun's internal ownership and safety guarantees.

## Why This Matters

Many framework-level operations are CPU-bound rather than network-bound.

title: `-filter` fails to match package whose directory name contains uppercase letter on Windows
excerpt:
### What version of Bun is running?

1.4.0-canary.1+ae4b17de6

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

When the root `package.json` declares `workspaces` with exact paths, `bun run --filter <name> <script>` fails to match package whose directory name contains uppercase ASCII letter.

The package is otherwise healthy: `bun install` resolves it, `bun pm ls` lists it, and `cd <dir> && bun run <script>` works.

Directory names use a mix of uppercase ASCII and CJK also trigger this, pure all-lowercase names do not.

Switching the same workspace to a glob declaration (`"packages/*"`) makes `--filter` work for all packages with no other changes.

Two failure modes:

1. **By exact name** → hard error: `error: No packages matched the filter` (exit 1)
2. **By wildcard `--filter '*'`** → the package is **silently skipped** (no error, exit 0), so a `--filter '*'` run quietly omits some packages

Repro:

```bash
mkdir repro && cd repro
mkdir -p packages/UpperPkg packages/lowerpkg

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "root",
  "private": true,
  "workspaces": ["packages/UpperPkg", "packages/lowerpkg"]
}
EOF

cat > packages/UpperPkg/package.json <<'EOF'
{ "name": "upper-pkg", "version": "0.0.0", "scripts": { "hi": "echo hello-from-upper" } }
EOF

cat > packages/lowerpkg/package.json <<'EOF'
{ "name": "lower-pkg", "version": "0.0.0", "scripts": { "hi": "echo hello-from-lower" } }
EOF

bun install
bun run --filter upper-pkg hi      # fails
bun run --filter '*' hi            # silently skips upper-pkg
```

```
$ bun pm ls
D:\repro node_modules (2)
├── lower-pkg@workspace:packages\lowerpkg
└── upper-pkg@workspace:packages\UpperPkg

$ bun run --filter lower-pkg hi        # lowercase dir name — works
lower-pkg hi: hello-from-lower
lower-pkg hi: Exited with code 0

$ bun run --filter upper-pkg hi        # UPPERCASE dir name — fails
error: No packages matched the filter

$ bun run --filter '*' hi              # silently skips upper-pkg
lower-pkg hi: hello-from-lower
lower-pkg hi: Exited with code 0
```

### What is the expected behavior?

`--filter` matching should be case-insensitive on Windows.

### What do you see instead?

_No response_

### Additional information

Reproduced on both Bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.0-canary.1

title: child_process.spawn throws ERR_UNKNOWN_ENCODING for options.encoding "buffer" (Node ignores it; breaks execa)
excerpt:
> [!NOTE]
> **AI-generated issue.** This bug was found, root-caused, and written up by an AI agent (Claude) while testing OpenClaw against Bun canary, on behalf of and reviewed by @steipete.

### What version of Bun is running?

`1.4.0-canary.1+43d60f69c` (Rust rewrite, current main) — also reproduces on stable `1.3.14` (Zig), so this is a longstanding Node-compat divergence, not a rewrite regression.

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 (Apple Silicon macOS)

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```js
const { spawn } = require("node:child_process");
const child = spawn("echo", ["hi"], { encoding: "buffer" });
child.stdout.on("data", (d) => console.log("data", d));
child.on("exit", (code) => console.log("exit", code));
```

Run with `bun repro.cjs`.

### What is the expected behavior?

Node's `child_process.spawn` does not have an `encoding` option and ignores unknown option keys:

```
$ node repro.cjs
data <Buffer 68 69 0a>
